stories.title: Susan Collins’ Hard-Luck Story Has An Assault-Rifle Twist
stories.text: Behind in the polls and with control of Congress possibly hinging on her reelection, incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins claimed in Tuesday’s closely watched Maine Senate debate that she’s experienced hard times. “I spent a year when I was running for governor in 1994, where I could not afford health insurance,” she said to her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, after he suggested the millionaire senator isn’t familiar with many Americans’ economic reality. Collins may have been cash-strapped while campaigning for Maine’s 1994 gubernatorial election. But within weeks of losing the race, she secured a high-profile new gig delivered by one of her campaign donors: assault-rifle manufacturer Richard Dyke. She would later vote to protect his business interests in Congress, stifling gun control regulation for decades. A month after the election, Collins was appointed founding executive director of the just-launched Richard E. Collins’ camp has tried to minimize Dyke’s role in her hiring, with a spokesperson telling ProPublica in 2023 that Husson’ president recruited her for the position. stories.text: Puntland security forces patrol after capturing ISIS bases in Cal Miskaad mountain range in Bari, east of the Gulf of Aden in the city of Bosasso, Puntland region, Somalia on January 25, 2025. REUTERS/Feisal Omar. MOGADISHU, Somalia—Drones had been hovering over Togga-Xarago—a mountainous settlement in northeastern Somalia all day. stories.title: Beware the Modern Wimp-Man
stories.text: Prince Harry: “I hated myself” Actor John Leguizamo, breaking down while receiving the Career Achievement Award from the Critics Choice Association: Leguizamo has been in a hundred movies and is fresh off a gift gig in the representation Olympics that was The Odyssey. He once boasted that voicing a dipshit sloth in the Ice Age series “got me a brownstone. It got me two extra homes, it got me a beautiful beachfront house in the Hamptons, it got me two pools!” and the next movie might buy “a helicopter” — and that was before he said that even if you “write like Shakespeare” but “look Latino,” the “odds are against you in Hollywood.” He’s whined that Spain’s Javier Bardem (thirty times the actor Leguizamo is) got parts in Before Night Falls and Being the Ricardos , railed against Antonio Banderas being cast in El Mariachi , and decried the choice of James Franco for the coveted role of Fidel Castro (“No more appropriation Hollywood… he ain’t Latino!”). stories.author: Judd Legum
stories.title: PopInfo Weekly: Mailers, measles, and manta ray
stories.text: This week, Popular Information released PaidForBy.info , a web app that gives unprecedented insight into who is really sending you political mailers — and who is paying for it. Anyone can use it for free. All you have to do is take a photo of the front and the back of the mailer and upload it. It also works on YouTube and TV ads. For months, Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and President Trump, have been claiming that Americans’ opposition to data centers is being manufactured by China. The claim was popularized by a 2026 report by the Bitcoin Policy Institute, which has been cited by several Republicans. The report, however, does not provide any evidence China is driving opposition to data centers. Through Paid For By , Popular Information obtained a political mailer from V-PAC, a super PAC supporting Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign for governor in Ohio, attacking his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. The mailer is rife with false and misleading claims. stories.title: Walmart Says It Prices Products, Not People. Its Patents Suggest Otherwise.
stories.text: Walmart serves 280 million shoppers a week and churned out more than $22 billion in profit in the last fiscal year. So, suffice it to say, I was floored – and maybe even a bit flattered – when the retail behemoth issued not one but two public responses in just over a week to the warnings I’ve made to shoppers about the retailer’s new surveillance pricing and price-gouging technologies in my new book and in recent interviews. In an open letter to customers from the CEO , followed by a letter from the company’s top PR executive addressing me directly, Walmart insists that it “price[s] products, not people” and argues that building technological capacity is not the same as deploying it. But here’s the problem: Walmart’s public assurances tell a very different story from the one buried in its patent filings. Walmart is pouring resources into developing and protecting the technology it needs to create intimate shopper profiles and use that data to shape what consumers pay. This week, our organization, Groundwork Collaborative, released a stunning analysis of more than 10 years of Walmart’s patent filings.
